seed_commits.message:
chore: initial project scaffold

FastAPI service, Postgres in compose and the CI skeleton. No assistant yet --
that is three years away.
seed_commits.author: Rosa Linnell <rosa.linnell@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(tickets): the ticket model and its store

Columns are named explicitly in every query. SELECT * is what lets a column added
to the table silently shift a field in the row tuple, and the symptom is a
requester email appearing in the assignee column six weeks later.
seed_commits.author: Rosa Linnell <rosa.linnell@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(tickets): SLA timers as pure functions

Every function takes `now` as an argument rather than reading a clock. That is
what lets the whole policy be tested with exact values instead of sleeps, and it
is why this module has never been the cause of a flaky test.

at_risk deliberately excludes what has already breached. Lumping the two
together makes the breached ones harder to find, not easier.
seed_commits.author: Rosa Linnell <rosa.linnell@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(db): one pooled connection helper, and only one

Everything goes through db.connection(). Tidiness is not the reason -- it is the
only way anything can later observe how long a connection is held, which turned
out to matter a great deal.

Pool size is 10 and stays 10. A generous pool hides the bug where a connection is
held across something slow: with 200 connections you need 200 concurrent requests
before anybody notices.
seed_commits.author: Idris Qureshi <idris.qureshi@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(tickets): search ranking and the service layer

The database filters and Python ranks. A few thousand live tickets is small enough
that an exact scan is free, and it keeps the ranking rules readable and testable
without a database.

Ties break by id so the order is total: two tickets with equal scores must not
swap places between two identical requests.
seed_commits.author: Idris Qureshi <idris.qureshi@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(tickets): the desk's own test suite

No model, no database. If any of these ever needs either, the layering has gone
wrong somewhere upstream of the test.
seed_commits.author: Idris Qureshi <idris.qureshi@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(serving): VRAM arithmetic for the model we are about to self-host

No accelerator and no torch: this is the planning layer, in exact integer arithmetic.
That is where production OOMs are actually caused -- the GPU did what it was told,
it was told wrong.

The leading 2 in the KV formula is a named constant so that dropping it is a
visible deletion in a diff rather than an invisible edit to a number. It is the
single most commonly dropped term in this calculation and it does not fail
loudly: it makes the planner believe it has twice the headroom it has.
seed_commits.author: Noor Abadi <noor.abadi@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(serving): paged KV cache instead of contiguous reservations

Reserving max_context per sequence wastes most of the card and fragments it: after
a few hundred requests there is plenty of free memory and no single free run large
enough to serve anybody.

Blocks are only returned by free(). Nothing reclaims them later and they are not
reference counted, so a path that finishes a request without calling it leaks
capacity for the life of the process -- no error, no crash, just a server that
admits fewer requests every hour. check_invariants() exists so that has somewhere
to be caught.
seed_commits.author: Noor Abadi <noor.abadi@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(serving): admission control reserves the peak

Two questions, two mechanisms. Reservation answers 'may this start' using prompt
plus every token the request may generate; the paged allocator answers 'where does
this token go' lazily.

Reserving on the prompt alone admits requests that each fit today and cannot all
fit at token 300. That failure lands mid-generation, after the user has been
streamed half an answer, and it is invisible in a load test with short replies.

Preemption evicts the newest request. Evicting the oldest maximizes the work
thrown away and punishes the longest wait.
seed_commits.author: Noor Abadi <noor.abadi@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(llm): the model, recorded

No live API call anywhere in this service. The key covers the tool contracts, the
observations so far, the question and the raw ticket text -- and deliberately not
the assembled prompt.

Keying on prompt bytes would mean any rewording turned every request into a miss,
so nobody could improve an instruction without re-recording the suite. Prompt
structure is checked by assertions instead.

Two circuit breakers, catching different failures: one for an agent stuck on a
single state, one for an agent that keeps moving and never stops. Without them a
broken loop hangs rather than failing, and a hung test tells you nothing.
seed_commits.author: Noor Abadi <noor.abadi@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(clock): pin the clock so recordings do not expire overnight

Tool output carries SLA state, SLA state reaches the cassette key. With a live
clock every recording in the repository would be stale tomorrow morning.

Production sets nothing and gets the real clock.
seed_commits.author: Noor Abadi <noor.abadi@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(assistant): tool registry, with validation at the boundary

Arguments arriving from a model are untrusted input, with the same standing as a
query string. The model is fluent, and fluency produces arguments that read
correctly and are not: a ticket id of 'the printer one', a status where a priority
belongs, a limit parameter the tool never declared.

Validation runs on every call so tool bodies may assume their arguments are
well-typed. The string form of an integer is accepted because a model told a
parameter is an integer still sometimes sends "42", and refusing that teaches
nothing.
seed_commits.author: Priya Nandakumar <priya.nandakumar@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(assistant): the tools, and the knowledge base they read

All read-only. The assistant drafts for a human to send; giving it a tool that
could change ticket state would be a product decision, not a technical one.

The knowledge base is a fixture rather than a table, so a policy question can
still be answered while the database is down.
seed_commits.author: Priya Nandakumar <priya.nandakumar@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(assistant): prompt assembly, with the catalog rendered from the registry

We kept a hand-written tool catalog here because it read more nicely. It drifted
within a month: search_tickets gained a limit parameter, the prose did not, and
the model spent three weeks never passing a limit while everybody assumed it had
decided five was enough. Nothing failed.

Untrusted text is fenced, and the fence neutralizes marker-shaped text in the
content. A fence that interpolates unchecked is theatre -- the attacker writes the
closing marker themselves and everything after it reads as operator instruction.
seed_commits.author: Priya Nandakumar <priya.nandakumar@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(assistant): the agent loop

The budget counts rounds, not successes. The tempting version increments only when
a tool succeeded, on the reasoning that a failed call did not really do anything.
It did: it cost a model call, and it is exactly the situation that repeats.

A tool result is appended as role=tool with the id of the call it answers. The
same characters in an assistant message are the model's own words quoted back at
it, so its request has not been served and it asks again.
seed_commits.author: Priya Nandakumar <priya.nandakumar@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(obs): probes, after the p95 test was deleted

The test that asserted p95 lasted two weeks. It failed on busy runners, got a
longer timeout, then another, and ended up asserting nothing anybody believed.
Worse, when it did fail it sent you to a profiler rather than to a line.

Every guarantee is now structural: whether a connection was open when a model call
started, which thread the model ran on, how many model calls a page made. Each is
exactly true or false on any machine under any load.
seed_commits.author: Idris Qureshi <idris.qureshi@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(assistant): where the assistant meets the request cycle

Read, release, generate off the loop, write. Fold the generation inside the read's
connection and ten concurrent assistant requests own the whole pool, at which
point the ticket list -- which never asked for an assistant -- starts timing out.

The dashboard reads the summary column and never regenerates. Regenerating is one
line, renders identically, and turns a 25-row page into 25 model calls.
seed_commits.author: Idris Qureshi <idris.qureshi@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(assistant): record the conversations

The transcript is the intent; `agentdesk cassettes` replays it against the real
tools to compute the keys. Hand-computing a key is error-prone in a way that fails
silently -- a key wrong by one character is a cassette nobody will ever read, and
the miss surfaces somewhere else entirely.

Ticket bodies are read from the seed rather than retyped, because the raw body is
part of the key.
seed_commits.author: Priya Nandakumar <priya.nandakumar@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat: HTTP surface and CLI

Every request model lives at module scope. With `from __future__ import
annotations` FastAPI resolves annotations against module globals, so a model
defined inside a function is invisible: the parameter stops being a body, becomes
a query parameter, and every POST returns 422 naming a field nobody wrote.

`agentdesk bench` prints timings for a human. Nothing gates on them.
seed_commits.author: Rosa Linnell <rosa.linnell@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
test: guard the layering and the cassette join

An architectural rule nothing checks is a comment. The import checks read source
rather than imported modules, because an import inside a function body is still an
import and is exactly the form the rule gets broken in.

The cassette join is checked in both directions. The reverse one is what catches
rot: a stale cassette is invisible, sitting there looking like coverage for a
conversation that can no longer happen.
seed_commits.author: Idris Qureshi <idris.qureshi@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
chore(ci): pipeline, and its executable mirror

There is no GitHub runner locally, so the workflow is the artifact you read and
run_ci.sh is what actually runs. Change one and you must change the other; a fix
applied to only one of them is incomplete, and the symptom is a pipeline green on
a laptop and red on a push.

The unit stage points DATABASE_URL and the proxies at dead ports. Anything that
has quietly acquired a connection or an HTTP call surfaces there rather than in
production as a timeout nobody can explain.
seed_commits.author: Rosa Linnell <rosa.linnell@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
docs: architecture, README and a notes skeleton

The module docstrings carry the reasoning. These three are the map.
seed_commits.author: Rosa Linnell <rosa.linnell@example.com>

setup_commands: make test    # expect failures: reproducing them is step one
make bench   # timings for a human; nothing is gated on them
